title: Java LinkedList
learningObjectives: Create a LinkedList using the List or Deque interface.
Add and remove elements at both ends.
Choose List for indexed sequence operations and Deque for operations at both ends when using LinkedList.

understand.concept: LinkedList is a doubly linked implementation of List and Deque. Each element is stored in a node linked to its neighbours. It supports efficient insertion and removal at the ends, and can act as a queue or deque. Indexed access requires traversal, so it is generally slower than ArrayList for frequent random reads. Choose a collection based on the operations the program performs rather than assuming one is always faster.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java linkedlist in maintainable applications.
understand.analogy: A LinkedList used as a Deque is like a line where people can join or leave at either end; the same structure can also be viewed as an ordered List.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not represent node allocation, reference links or the cost of indexed traversal.

explain.narrative:
LinkedList implements both List and Deque. Methods such as addFirst, addLast, getFirst, removeFirst and peekLast express end operations clearly. As a queue, offer adds and poll retrieves/removes the head. A Deque supports both ends and can model a queue or stack. Be careful with methods that throw when empty, such as getFirst; peekFirst returns null instead. The data structure choice should follow access patterns and measured needs.

## List and Deque views of LinkedList

LinkedList implements both `List<E>` and `Deque<E>`. Use a `List<E>` reference when the requirement is an ordered sequence with index-based operations. Use a `Deque<E>` reference when the requirement is adding or removing at either end, such as a queue or stack. Choosing the interface communicates the operations the rest of the program is allowed to depend on.

examples.title: Add at both ends
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> line = new LinkedList<>(); line.add("B"); line.addFirst("A"); line.addLast("C"); System.out.println(line); } }
examples.explanation: LinkedList offers methods for inserting at either end.

examples.title: Read the ends
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.add(10); q.add(20); System.out.println(q.getFirst()); System.out.println(q.getLast()); } }
examples.explanation: getFirst and getLast inspect the two ends.

examples.title: Remove the first item
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.add("Job1"); q.add("Job2"); System.out.println(q.removeFirst()); System.out.println(q); } }
examples.explanation: removeFirst removes and returns the head element.

examples.title: Use as a queue
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer("Print"); q.offer("Scan"); System.out.println(q.poll()); System.out.println(q.peek()); } }
examples.explanation: offer, poll and peek are queue-style operations.

examples.title: Use LinkedList through Deque
examples.code:
import java.util.Deque; import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Deque<String> jobs = new LinkedList<>(); jobs.offerLast("Print"); jobs.offerLast("Scan"); System.out.println(jobs.pollFirst()); System.out.println(jobs.peekFirst()); } }
examples.explanation: Deque expresses operations at both ends. LinkedList implements Deque; pollFirst removes and returns the head while peekFirst inspects the new head.

practise.guidedTask: Declare a Deque<String> backed by LinkedList. Use offerLast to add jobs, peekFirst to inspect the next job, and pollFirst to remove it. Then demonstrate addFirst and removeLast to show operations at both ends.
practise.independentTask: Create a task queue that handles an empty queue safely. Compare pollFirst and removeFirst when the deque is empty, and explain why the former returns null while the latter throws an exception.
hints: LinkedList implements both List and Deque; choose the interface based on whether the code needs positional list operations or queue/deque operations.
Indexed access in LinkedList requires traversal, so repeated get(index) in a loop can be inefficient.
Use iterator or deque operations for sequential processing and compare with ArrayList for the actual access pattern.
practise.challenge: Explain when a LinkedList should be referenced as List and when it should be referenced as Deque. Compare its API guarantees with ArrayList and avoid claiming that LinkedList is always faster.

questions.explanation: LinkedList supports both List and Deque operations.

questions.prompt: Which operation adds at the front?
What does poll() do on a queue?
questions.answer: Returns and removes the head, or null if empty
options: Returns and removes the head, or null if empty
questions.explanation: poll is a non-throwing retrieval-and-removal operation.

questions.prompt: Which access pattern is generally better suited to ArrayList?
questions.explanation: ArrayList offers constant-time indexed access in typical use.

questions.prompt: Which interface best communicates that a collection is used for operations at both ends?
questions.explanation: Deque defines insertion, retrieval and removal operations at both ends.
